newsitem.title: FRANCE: Albright says U.S. to keep global role-French paper.
newsitem.headline: Albright says U.S. to keep global role-French paper.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, speaking to a French newspaper ahead of her first overseas tour since taking office, said she wanted European allies to understand Washington would continue to shoulder world responsibilities.

"I want the Europeans to see me as the representative of an America which is well and truly convinced that it has global responsibilities...," Albright told Le Monde in an interview published on Saturday.

"...This means that when we can make things change, we will do so. The other part of the messaage is that the United States also wants to act, each time it is possible, together with its allies, in a sort of co-responsibility, " she said.
Albright will be in Paris on Monday as part of an 11-day trip taking her to Europe and Asia. She will also be making stops in Rome, Bonn, Brussels, London, Moscow, Seoul, Tokyo and Beijing.

Asked about accusations of U.S. arrogance in world afffairs, she said Washington was blamed if it acted and equally blamed if it failed to act in major crises. "I think it is very important that one understand America's responsibilities are inherent to its size and power.
"Certain countries like to maintain the perception that America is arrogant in order to make themselves out to be victims," she said.
Turning to relations with France which have been frayed over a series of issues ranging from NATO to Africa, she said: "Franco-American relations are of capital importance for us.

"France is our oldest ally and my experience at the United Nations was that when France and the U.S. worked together, we both benefitted. Obviously there are areas where we disagree because we each have our own national interests. But the aim of my visit is to develop points of convergence," she said.
Albright confirmed the U.S. had no intention of giving up NATO's southern command which Paris would like to see attributed to a European officer.

She also called for closer ties between the European Union and the Baltic states and said the U.S. would tighten its own links with the Ukraine and seek to convince Russia of the merits of cooperation over Europe.

In past decades, France's fiercely independent foreign policy, drawing on a colonial past and its tradition as a cradle of human rights, often allowed it to stake out a respectable middle ground between the superpowers.
But the collapse of the Soviet Union means France's positions now often sound more like bickering with Washington than brokering.
